title: Kaliningrad: Russia's Exclave Ringed by NATO, German Until 1945

thumbnail.idea: True-colour satellite view of the south-east Baltic. Kaliningrad is outlined in a thick red line with a red marker on the city. The 65 km strip between its south-east corner and Belarus is circled in red, with a dashed white measuring line across it. A big dashed arrow runs from the Russian mainland toward Kaliningrad and stops short at the Lithuanian border. Compact text block top-left.

minor: 'The line drawn: when the USSR dissolved in 1991, Kaliningrad became an exclave' - the exclave status began when Lithuania's independence was recognised in September 1991. The USSR dissolved in December. Say 'when Lithuania left the USSR'.

'On 18 June 2022, Lithuania stopped rail shipments' - the Lithuanian Railways notice is dated 17 June and the ban took effect at the turn of 17-18 June. The listed source dates it 18 June, so this is consistent with the source.

The shot tagged (quote), 'In 1990, the treaty that reunited Germany settled the old question...', is a paraphrase of Article 1(3), not a quotation. Either retag it as a document or read the article's wording aloud.

'If your country is among NATO's 32, your army is pledged to defend it.' - 'it' is ambiguous. Article 5 pledges the defence of members, not of Kaliningrad or the strip of land. Name the object, e.g. 'pledged to defend that strip'.

'Its borders with Poland and Lithuania were drawn in their present form in 1945-46' - Potsdam was provisional, and the Soviet-Polish line was demarcated and adjusted into the late 1940s and 1950s. Soften to 'were set in 1945-46'.

'What left it unreachable overland was Lithuania's independence in 1991' is a simplification. Poland's border and Belarus's independence also matter, and the declaration came in 1990. Consider 'above all'.
'Kalinin, a senior Soviet official' is acceptable. He was the nominal head of state, so 'long-time Soviet head of state' is more exact.

shots.vo: This is Kaliningrad. Until 1945 this city was the German Königsberg.
How did Russia end up with a once-German city it can't reach overland?
The answer starts in 1758, the first time Russia ruled this city.

shots.vo: Kaliningrad sits on the south-east shore of the Baltic Sea, with Poland to the south and Lithuania to the north and east.
The CIA World Factbook measures its land border with Poland at 209 kilometres, and with Lithuania at 261.
Moscow is about 1,090 kilometres away in a straight line, and every road there crosses at least one other country.
Russia's 2021 census counted about 1.03 million people here, nearly half of them in the city of Kaliningrad.
The city stands on the Pregolya river, joined to the open sea by a ship canal 43 kilometres long.
At the canal's mouth is Baltiysk, the main base of Russia's Baltic Fleet and its westernmost naval port.
The same narrow strait is the only natural exit from the Vistula Lagoon, which Russia shares with Poland.
So for decades, ships bound for the Polish port of Elbląg had to pass through Russian waters to reach the Baltic.
To the north, the Curonian Spit, a 98-kilometre ribbon of dunes, is split between Russia and Lithuania.
Beneath the coast lies amber: the state-owned Kaliningrad Amber Combine says the region holds about 90 per cent of the world's reserves.

stat.label: share of world amber reserves, per Kaliningrad Amber Combine, 2021

shots.vo: Overland, Russian trains reach the region only by crossing Lithuania, on a line that continues into Belarus.
The other way in is by sea: cargo ferries run from Ust-Luga, near St Petersburg.
Since Sweden joined NATO in March 2024, every Baltic shore except Russia's own two stretches belongs to an alliance member.
And since February 2025, when the Baltic states left the Russian-run power grid for Europe's, the region has run its own grid alone.
Between Kaliningrad and Belarus, Russia's closest ally, lies the Polish-Lithuanian border: 104 kilometres long.
Measured straight across, the distance is about 65 kilometres. NATO planners call it the Suwałki gap, after a nearby Polish town.
It is the only land route between the three Baltic states and the rest of NATO.
Its borders with Poland and Lithuania were drawn in their present form in 1945–46. So who drew them, and why did Russia get the city?
Teutonic Knights founded Königsberg in 1255. By tradition, it was named after King Ottokar II of Bohemia, who joined their campaign.
In 1525 it became capital of the Duchy of Prussia, and in 1701 Prussia's first king was crowned here.
Moment one came in January 1758, during the Seven Years' War, when Russian troops entered the city.

shots.vo: East Prussia was governed from St Petersburg for four years, and its people swore allegiance to Empress Elizabeth.
Immanuel Kant, then a young lecturer, petitioned the empress for a professorship. He did not get it.

shots.vo: In 1762 a new tsar, Peter III, made peace with Prussia and handed the province back. The line drawn: Russian occupation ended.
Moment two began after the First World War. The Treaty of Versailles gave Poland a corridor to the sea.
East Prussia was now cut off from the rest of Germany. Germans reached it by sea, or by sealed trains across Poland.
In August 1944, British bombers destroyed much of the old city centre.

shots.vo: On 9 April 1945, after a siege, the German garrison surrendered to the Soviet army.

headline.text: Königsberg garrison surrenders to Soviet forces

shots.vo: That summer, at Potsdam, outside Berlin, Soviet, American and British leaders discussed Germany's eastern borders.
They agreed 'in principle' that the city and the land around it would pass to the Soviet Union, pending a final peace settlement.

document.title: Protocol of the Proceedings of the Berlin (Potsdam) Conference, 1 August 1945, Section VI
document.highlight: The Conference has agreed in principle to the proposal of the Soviet Government concerning the ultimate transfer to the Soviet Union of the City of Koenigsberg and the area adjacent to it as described above subject to expert examination of the actual frontier.

shots.vo: The line drawn: East Prussia was cut in two, the north to the Soviet Union and the south under Polish administration, with the Memel area attached to Soviet Lithuania.
In July 1946 the city was renamed Kaliningrad, after Mikhail Kalinin, a senior Soviet official who had died weeks earlier.
By 1948 the remaining German residents had been deported to Germany, and settlers from across the Soviet Union replaced them.

shots.vo: Inside the Soviet Union, the separation hardly mattered: Lithuania was a Soviet republic too, and the region lay inside one country.
In 1990, the treaty that reunited Germany settled the old question: Germany renounced any claim to other states' territory.

quote.text: The united Germany has no territorial claims whatsoever against other states and shall not assert any in the future.
quote.who: Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany, Article 1(3)

shots.vo: Moment three began when Lithuania declared independence in March 1990; Moscow recognised it in September 1991.
The line drawn: when the USSR dissolved in 1991, Kaliningrad became an exclave, cut off from the rest of Russia by a foreign border.
Poland joined NATO in 1999. Lithuania followed in 2004, the same year both joined the European Union.
A Russian region was now surrounded by the alliance Moscow had faced for decades. Each side reads that map differently.

map.label: Surrounded by NATO and the EU

shots.vo: In 2002, Russia and the EU agreed a transit deal: Russians could cross Lithuania with a simple document instead of a visa.

headline.text: EU and Russia agree simplified transit for Kaliningrad

shots.vo: Trains between Kaliningrad and the rest of Russia kept running through Lithuania under that deal.
In February 2018, Vladimir Shamanov, head of the Russian parliament's defence committee, said Iskander missiles were deployed in the region.

headline.text: Russian MP confirms Iskander missiles in Kaliningrad

shots.vo: Russia gives the Iskander's range as up to 500 kilometres. Warsaw is about 280 kilometres from Kaliningrad.

map.label: ≈280 km · stated range up to 500 km

shots.vo: NATO had already moved: at its 2016 Warsaw summit, it agreed to station multinational battlegroups in Poland and the three Baltic states.
In April 2025, Germany formally commissioned a brigade in Lithuania, its first permanent unit based abroad since the Second World War.
The German army plans about 4,800 soldiers there by 2027.

stat.label: planned German brigade in Lithuania by 2027

shots.vo: On 18 June 2022, Lithuania stopped rail shipments of EU-sanctioned goods to Kaliningrad, starting with steel and other metals.

headline.text: Sanctioned steel stopped at Lithuania's border with Kaliningrad

shots.vo: The region's governor, Anton Alikhanov, said 40 to 50 per cent of its imports were affected.

stat.label: share of Kaliningrad imports affected, per its governor, June 2022

shots.vo: Russia's case, at its strongest: the 2002 deal guaranteed transit between two parts of one country, and its Foreign Ministry called the ban a breach.
Moscow also says NATO forces on the region's borders are the threat, and that its own deployments there respond to them.
Lithuania's case, at its strongest: it was applying EU sanctions, not its own, while passengers and unsanctioned freight kept moving.
On 13 July 2022, the European Commission said sanctioned goods could cross by rail but not by road, and military goods not at all.

headline.text: Brussels clears sanctioned rail freight to Kaliningrad, not by road

shots.vo: Poland, which said it wanted to end its dependence on Russian waters, opened its own canal on 17 September 2022.
Ships for Elbląg can now reach the Baltic without passing through Russian waters.
In May 2023, a Polish naming commission recommended calling the city by its historical Polish name, Królewiec.
And NATO figures show Poland's defence spending rose from under 2 per cent of its economy in 2014 to almost 4.5 per cent in 2025.

chart.title: Poland more than doubled
chart.source: NATO, Defence Expenditure of NATO Countries, June 2025

shots.vo: Since 2024, Poland's East Shield and the Baltic states' joint defence line have begun fortifying their borders with Russia and Belarus.
Poland set aside about 10 billion zloty for East Shield, to be finished by 2028.

stat.label: Poland's East Shield budget, announced May 2024

shots.vo: Both sides are now building along this same frontier. Where that leads is still open.
None of what follows is a prediction. These are three paths analysts discuss, and what each would do to the map.
Path one: the gap hardens. Brigades, barriers and exercises thicken on both sides of the 65 kilometres.
Planners study this ground closely. In a 2016 RAND wargame, Russian forces reached the outskirts of Tallinn or Riga in 60 hours at most.

document.title: RAND, 'Reinforcing Deterrence on NATO's Eastern Flank: Wargaming the Defense of the Baltics', 2016
document.highlight: The longest it has taken Russian forces to reach the outskirts of the Estonian and/or Latvian capitals of Tallinn and Riga, respectively, is 60 hours.

shots.vo: That study predates NATO's forward battlegroups. And Russia's president said in February 2024 that Russia had no interest in Poland, Latvia or anywhere else.
On this path, the map would show one of Europe's most fortified borders, with Kaliningrad an armed island inside it.
Path two: transit narrows. If the EU extended its rail restrictions, more of the region's supplies would have to come by sea.
Its lifeline would then be the ferry route from Ust-Luga, through waters bordered by NATO members almost the whole way.
On the map, the rail line through Lithuania would fade, and the sea lane would become the region's only steady link.
Path three: a thaw. From 2012 to 2016, residents of the whole region could cross into a Polish border zone without visas.
That Polish zone reached as far as Gdańsk. Poland suspended the scheme in July 2016 and has not restored it.
On this path, the borders would open again, and the region would face its neighbours rather than its fences.
Each path runs through the same 65 kilometres, and none of them is decided in Kaliningrad alone.
So Russia does not own a piece of Germany. It holds what the Allies agreed in principle in 1945 and Germany renounced in 1990.
What left it unreachable overland was Lithuania's independence in 1991, whose border now sits on its only rail route.
Next: a strait about 700 metres wide at its narrowest, where a 1936 treaty lets Turkey regulate which warships pass.
